messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Anwar Rahman, an 80-year-old widowed South Eastern Asian man who had spent much of his working life as a data scientist, came to treatment describing a fear that had narrowed his world since his time as a relief worker in a war zone. He could still picture one night in particular: a crowded shelter with broken lights, shouting outside, families pressed into corners, and his team unable to move people to safety because armed men had blocked the only road out. The sense of having no options in that moment had stayed with him, and now even ordinary encounters could pull him back to it. If he saw people misbehaving in a store, arguing loudly on the street, or dismissing rules as if they did not apply to them, he felt the old alarm rise immediately. The same happened when he woke from a nightmare in a sweat, disoriented for a few seconds, still caught between sleep and the present. In those moments, Mr. Rahman would begin scanning the room, checking exits and windows, and mentally rehearsing what to say before speaking to anyone, as though careful preparation could keep the world from turning dangerous.

He described the memory itself as having an unnerving quality that made it impossible to place in the past. When he remembered the event, he did not experience it as something he had survived and left behind; he felt as if it was happening right now, like a film playing over and over with no break. The sounds, the pressure in his chest, and the feeling of being trapped returned with such force that his body reacted before he could reason with it. These memory surges were often followed by the same conclusion: if his reactions were this intense, perhaps he was going crazy. He had become frightened by his own anger as well, worrying that one day he would not be able to control it and would do something terrible. That fear of himself sat alongside a broader conviction that the world was dangerous, a place where violence and humiliation could erupt without warning. The more his mind returned to the war-zone scene, the more certain he became that danger was not over but waiting.

Over the months that followed, Mr. Rahman’s attempts to manage that dread made his symptoms more entrenched. He avoided news reports about events similar to what had happened to him, telling himself that he could not afford to let those images in. Yet when he did encounter a headline or a broadcast, even briefly, the familiar shelter scene flooded back with startling force, and his memories became vivid again, as if the old film had been started from the beginning. The same was true of encounters that echoed the original trap: a crowded hallway, a blocked doorway, or a situation where he felt there were no choices. Those moments were potent because they carried the same helplessness he had known in the war zone, and they immediately stirred the present-tense memory of being trapped. After one such episode in the lobby of his apartment building, he spent the rest of the day replaying the event in his mind and checking the surroundings every few minutes, trying to prevent a repeat. But the more he rehearsed and monitored, the more tightly the frightening scene seemed to cling to him, making the memory feel even less like something finished.

At work, where he still consulted part-time from home on data projects, Mr. Rahman found himself rehearsing conversations before every call and every meeting, worrying that a careless word or a sudden irritation would expose how unsettled he felt. He would spend long stretches scanning the environment around his desk, listening for raised voices in the building and watching the hallway through his door crack. Yet these efforts also kept the fear alive; each time he checked for danger, he was reminded that danger might be near, and each rehearsal confirmed how unsteady he believed himself to be. He came to the painful conclusion that his reactions meant he was losing his mind, and that belief deepened his anger and shame. A nightmare followed by waking in the dark would leave him tense and suspicious for the rest of the morning, and the next news bulletin or quarrel in the neighborhood would reopen the same memory. Over time he withdrew from social contact, spoke less with neighbors, and became increasingly isolated in his apartment, where the constant vigilance exhausted him.

By the time he sought help, Mr. Rahman was no longer only frightened by what had happened overseas; he was frightened by the way his mind kept bringing it back, by the anger he felt in his body, and by the possibility that he might become someone dangerous himself. What finally brought him in was his growing concern that the cycle was tightening around him: the nightmares, the scanning, the avoidance, and the replaying were leaving him more tense, more irritable, and more convinced that he could not trust either the world or his own reactions. He said he wanted relief, but what he feared most was that this would keep happening for the rest of his life and that he would end up alone, ruled by a danger that never truly stayed in the past.
